title: Cheapest way to connect every vertex
description:
A set of offices has to be wired into a single network. Each possible cable joins two offices and has a non-negative cost. A network is a choice of cables that lets every office reach every other one, directly or through other offices, and its cost is the sum of the cables chosen.

Implement a struct type called Edge with two integer fields: To, the vertex at the other end of the edge, and Weight, its cost. Then implement a function called CheapestNetworkCost that receives the number of vertices and an adjacency list, and returns the cost of the cheapest network. Vertices are numbered from zero. The adjacency list gives, for each vertex, the edges leaving it, and every edge appears in both directions.

With the edges 0-1 (cost 4), 0-2 (8), 1-2 (3), 1-4 (6), 2-3 (2), 3-4 (10):
CheapestNetworkCost(5, adjacency) -> 15. The cheapest network keeps 2-3, 1-2, 0-1 and 1-4, for 2 + 3 + 4 + 6 = 15.

What counts is the weight of each edge on its own, not how far a vertex ends up from wherever you started. With the edges 0-1 (2), 1-2 (2), 0-2 (3), CheapestNetworkCost(3, adjacency) -> 4: the cheapest network keeps 0-1 and 1-2, even though vertex 2 is closer to vertex 0 through the direct edge of 3.

If the cables cannot connect every office, no network exists, and the result is -1: with only the edge 0-1 (cost 3) among three vertices, CheapestNetworkCost(3, adjacency) -> -1. A graph with a single vertex needs no edges at all, so its result is 0.

The hidden tests also check parallel edges between the same two vertices, where only the cheapest one can be worth keeping; edges of cost zero; and an expensive edge that must be kept because it is the only way to reach a vertex.

This card asks for the optimal solution, and the tests enforce it: one of them is a graph of two hundred thousand vertices with a two second budget. Scanning every vertex on each step to find the one that is cheapest to attach gives the right answer but is far too slow to pass. The next vertex to attach has to come out of a priority queue, and the total work has to stay close to the number of edges times the logarithm of the number of vertices.
objective: Recall and implement Prim's minimum spanning tree algorithm with a min-heap keyed on edge weight, including skipping vertices already in the tree and detecting a disconnected graph.
